Newborn Care

How to Prepare Baby Formula Safely: Water and Mixing

Updated: August 5, 2026

Written and edited by Mohammadamin Namyar, founder of BeMama — checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

To prepare baby formula safely, wash your hands, boil fresh water and let it cool briefly so it is still at least 70 degrees Celsius, pour the measured water into a clean bottle, add level unpacked scoops exactly as the label directs, shake, then cool the bottle and test it on your wrist before feeding. Those steps exist because powdered formula is not sterile, and a few consistent habits protect young babies from rare but serious infections. This guide walks through the four moments that matter: preparing, feeding, storing, and cleaning.

Why the preparation rules exist

Powdered infant formula is not sterile, even when the tin is sealed and well within its date. Very rarely, powder can contain a germ called Cronobacter, which can cause serious bloodstream or brain infections in very young babies. The risk is highest for babies under about 2 months old, babies born prematurely, and babies with weakened immune systems. That is the whole reason preparation rules exist: hot enough water, exact measuring, and short standing times shrink an already small risk to something much smaller. None of this means formula is unsafe. Enormous numbers of babies are formula fed and thrive. It simply means a few habits are worth doing the same way every single time.

If your baby is in one of those higher-risk groups, sterile liquid formula is the safest option, because the Cronobacter risk comes mainly from powder. Ready-to-feed bottles are sterile until you open them, and liquid concentrate is also sterile before mixing. Some families use ready-to-feed for the first weeks and switch to powder later, or keep a few bottles on hand for nights and travel. If cost makes liquid formula unrealistic, careful powder preparation with hot water, described below, is a reasonable and widely recommended approach. Talk with your pediatric team if your baby was premature or has a medical condition, since they may prefer sterile liquid for longer.

Choose your water

In most cities and towns, plain tap water that is safe for you to drink is also an acceptable base for formula, which is consistent with CDC guidance. If you use well water, have it tested before using it for a baby, and ask your local health department how often to retest. Bottled water is fine too, but it is not sterile, so it follows the same handling rules as tap water. If your home has older plumbing, run the cold tap briefly before filling the kettle, and always start from the cold tap rather than the hot one. If you are unsure about your supply, your baby's clinician or local public health office can advise you.

For babies under about 2 months, premature babies, and babies with weakened immune systems, the WHO and the NHS advise mixing powder with water that has been boiled and then cooled for no more than about 30 minutes, so it is still at least 70 degrees Celsius, about 158 Fahrenheit. Water that hot kills Cronobacter that may be present in the powder itself. Boil fresh water, let it sit briefly, pour the measured amount into a clean bottle, then add the powder. For older, healthy babies, many families mix powder with safe room-temperature water instead. Ask your pediatrician which approach fits your baby and your situation.

Measure and mix exactly as the label says

Follow the ratio on your container exactly, and always put the water in the bottle first, then the powder. Use only the scoop that came in that specific container, since scoop sizes differ between brands and even between products from the same brand. Fill the scoop loosely and level it off with a clean knife; never pack it down or add a little extra for a hungrier baby. Never dilute formula to stretch a can. Extra water can cause poor growth and, in young babies, dangerous drops in blood sodium, while extra powder can strain the kidneys and cause dehydration. The printed ratio is the safe zone, so treat it like a recipe you never improvise.

Cap the bottle and shake or swirl until the powder fully dissolves. If you mixed with hot water, cool the bottle quickly by holding it under cold running water or standing it in a bowl of cold water, keeping the water level below the ring so nothing splashes onto the nipple. Test a few drops on the inside of your wrist before feeding; the milk should feel warm or barely lukewarm, never hot. Do not warm any bottle in a microwave. Microwaves heat unevenly and can leave scalding pockets in milk that feels cool on the outside. A jug of warm water or a bottle warmer used as directed is the safer route.

The timing rules, all in one place

Once formula is mixed, a simple clock starts. Use the bottle within 2 hours of preparing it if it stays at room temperature, and within 1 hour of the moment your baby starts drinking. After a feed begins, bacteria from your baby's mouth travel back into the milk, so anything left after about an hour goes down the drain, even if it looks untouched. Do not put a partly finished bottle back in the fridge for later, and do not top it up with fresh formula. If a freshly mixed bottle has not been offered at all and less than 2 hours have passed, you can still refrigerate it promptly and use it later.

Preparing ahead can save your sanity at night. Mix bottles, cool them fast, and put them straight into the back of the refrigerator, not the door; use them within 24 hours. Warm a chilled bottle once and never rewarm it. For outings, the safest options are ready-to-feed bottles or a flask of hot water plus powder measured into a clean container, mixed fresh when your baby is hungry. Tired brains lose track of timing easily, so write the mixing time on a strip of tape on each bottle, or note feed times in the BeMama app or a notebook so 2 hours never quietly becomes 5.

Keep hands, bottles, and surfaces clean

Clean hands and clean gear do a surprising amount of the work. Wash your hands with soap and water for about 20 seconds before preparing any bottle, and wipe down the counter you mix on. After every feed, take the bottle, nipple, and ring apart and wash them in hot soapy water with a brush kept only for baby items, or run them through the dishwasher on a hot cycle with heated drying. Rinse everything first so milk residue does not bake on. Let the pieces air dry completely on a clean rack or towel; rubbing the inside with a dish towel can add germs rather than remove them.

Sanitizing goes one step beyond washing and matters most for babies under about 2 months, premature babies, and babies with weakened immune systems; the CDC suggests sanitizing at least once a day for these groups. Boil the clean parts for about 5 minutes, use a steam sterilizer as directed, or run a dishwasher sanitize cycle. Older healthy babies usually do fine with thorough washing alone. Know the escalation signs too: a temperature of 38 degrees Celsius, 100.4 Fahrenheit, or higher in a baby under 3 months is urgent, so call your clinician right away rather than waiting. Seek emergency care if your baby is unusually floppy, hard to wake, breathing with difficulty, refusing feeds, or vomiting repeatedly, since these can signal serious infection in a young baby.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

Formula preparation requires hand hygiene, clean equipment, safe water, and the exact water-to-formula ratio on the container. Powdered formula is not sterile, and some young or medically vulnerable babies need additional precautions.

Bottle feeding can be responsive: hold the baby, watch hunger and fullness cues, pause as needed, and never prop a bottle. Storage and discard times apply even when a bottle still looks or smells normal.

How BeMama can help

Use BeMama to coordinate bottle times, amounts, formula type, and preparation notes. It cannot verify mixing, storage temperature, product safety, or the right amount for a baby.

When to seek help

Contact a healthcare professional for a possible mixing error, poor feeding, repeated vomiting, unusual sleepiness, dehydration concerns, or fever.

Sources and further reading

  • CDC — Infant Formula Preparation and Storage
  • WHO — Infant and young child feeding

Links lead directly to guidance from the organizations named above.

Key takeaways

  • Powdered formula is not sterile, so careful preparation matters most in the first 2 months.
  • For young or high-risk babies, mix powder with water still at least 70 degrees Celsius, or use sterile ready-to-feed formula.
  • Add water first, use level unpacked scoops, and never dilute or concentrate formula.
  • Use mixed formula within 2 hours, within 1 hour once a feed starts, and discard leftovers.
  • Wash hands and bottle parts after every feed, sanitize daily for young babies, and never microwave a bottle.

Frequently asked questions

Do you need to boil water for baby formula?

Yes, if your baby is under about 2 months old, premature, or has a weakened immune system: the WHO and NHS advise mixing powder with freshly boiled water cooled for no more than about 30 minutes, so it is still at least 70 degrees Celsius. That temperature kills Cronobacter that can occasionally be present in the powder itself. For older, healthy babies, safe tap or bottled water at room temperature is generally acceptable. Ask your pediatrician which approach fits your baby and your local water supply.

How long is formula good after mixing?

Prepared formula is good for up to 2 hours at room temperature, or up to 24 hours if you refrigerate it immediately after mixing. Once your baby starts drinking from the bottle, the window shrinks to about 1 hour. Store made-ahead bottles at the back of the fridge, not in the door, and warm each one only once.

Can you reuse formula after baby drinks from the bottle?

No, discard whatever is left within about 1 hour of the start of the feed. Bacteria from your baby's mouth enter the milk while drinking and can multiply, even in the refrigerator. To waste less, offer smaller amounts per bottle and mix a little more if your baby still seems hungry.

How do you sterilize baby bottles?

Wash the bottle parts first, then boil them for about 5 minutes, use a steam sterilizer as directed, or run a dishwasher sanitize cycle. Sanitize at least once a day for babies under about 2 months, premature babies, and babies with weakened immune systems. Let everything air dry on a clean rack rather than towel-drying the insides. Older healthy babies usually do fine with careful washing in hot soapy water after every feed.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
